The metabolomics profiling reveals a pronounced perturbation in **Biological Oxidations (Reactome R-HSA-211859)**, the top candidate pathway by hypergeometric enrichment (FDR = 0.0, fold-enrichment = 128.5×). Seven of the nine differentially abundant metabolites — L-Cysteine (C00097), bromide (C01324), coumarin (C05851), benzo[a]pyrene-7,8-dihydrodiol-9,10-epoxide (C14853), N-hydroxy-4-aminobiphenyl (C20319), methimazole (C07190), and β-mercaptoethanol (C00928) — map to this pathway. The companion pathway **Phase II – Conjugation of Compounds (R-HSA-156580)** is likewise significantly enriched (FDR = 0.0, fold-enrichment = 159×), with four drivers — L-Cysteine, benzo[a]pyrene-7,8-dihydrodiol-9,10-epoxide, N-hydroxy-4-aminobiphenyl, and β-mercaptoethanol — confirmed as members via database lookup.

The most plausible biological interpretation is that the treatment has induced or inhibited a xenobiotic-metabolising enzyme system, most likely the cytochrome P450 family, which orchestrates Phase I oxidations and feeds substrates into Phase II conjugation. The simultaneous elevation of coumarin (a known CYP2A6 substrate and probe compound), the polyaromatic hydrocarbon diol epoxide (a CYP1A1/1B1 activation product of benzo[a]pyrene), and the arylamine N-hydroxy metabolite points to generalised induction of oxidative xenobiotic metabolism. L-Cysteine's presence in both pathways reflects its role as a conjugating substrate for glutathione S-transferase and N-acetyltransferase reactions, suggesting heightened nucleophilic scavenging capacity. Methimazole — an antithyroid drug and known CYP inhibitor — may itself be a treatment agent whose metabolic fate is being tracked. Dihydrobiopterin (C02953) and 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid (C00632), while not matched to the top-ranked Reactome entries, are consistent with oxidative stress and tryptophan-kynurenine pathway activation. The upstream/downstream relationships among these xenobiotics could not be formally verified within the KEGG reaction graph due to sparse connectivity for several compounds, but the shared pathway context is robust.

In summary, the treatment group is characterised by a coordinated elevation of Phase I oxidation and Phase II conjugation metabolites, indicative of either enzyme induction (e.g., AhR-mediated CYP1A upregulation) or a shift in xenobiotic load that the liver is actively processing. This pattern warrants targeted CYP enzyme activity assays and oxidative stress biomarkers for mechanistic follow-up.
